docs/adding-a-server.heading: Adding a server
docs/adding-a-server.intro: Every connection in VVTerm starts with a server entry. Here is what each field means, how servers belong to workspaces and environments, and how to edit or delete them.
docs/adding-a-server.title: Adding a server in VVTerm — VVTerm
docs/adding-a-server.description: Learn the server fields in VVTerm — name, host, port, username, and environment — how servers belong to workspaces, and how to edit or delete them.
docs/adding-a-server.schemaDescription: How to add a server in VVTerm: name, host, port, username, and environment, plus how servers belong to workspaces and how to edit or delete them.
docs/adding-a-server.bodyHtml:
A server in VVTerm is the saved definition of a machine you connect to: where it lives, who you log in as, and how you authenticate. Once saved, it appears in your server list and syncs across your devices through iCloud. Credentials themselves stay in the Apple Keychain and are never part of that synced definition.

Server fields

  • Name — a label you choose so the server is easy to recognize. It has no effect on the connection.
  • Host — the hostname or IP address to connect to, for example example.com or 192.168.1.20.
  • Port — the SSH port. This defaults to 22; change it only if your server listens on a different port.
  • Username — the account you log in as, such as root, ubuntu, or admin.
  • Environment — an optional grouping, like Production or Staging, used to organize servers inside a workspace.

Authentication is set per server. You can use a password, an SSH key, or an SSH key protected by a passphrase. The details and where each credential is stored are covered in Authentication and SSH keys.

Workspaces and environments

Every server belongs to a workspace. A workspace is a top-level group — you might keep one workspace per client, per project, or per team. Inside a workspace, an environment further sorts servers so you can keep production and staging hosts visually separate and filter the list down to what you need.

On the free tier you get one workspace and one server. Pro removes those limits so you can build out as many workspaces, environments, and servers as you like. See Workspaces, environments, and tabs for how this fits together with multiple open connections.

Editing a server

  1. Open the server's details from your list.
  2. Change any field — name, host, port, username, environment, or the authentication method.
  3. Save. The updated definition syncs to your other devices through iCloud.

Changing the host, port, or username affects only future connections. If a session is already open, it keeps its original settings until you reconnect.

Deleting a server

Deleting a server removes its definition from your list and, after sync, from your other devices. Any keychain credential tied to the server is removed with it. If you only want to stop seeing a server temporarily, consider moving it to a different environment instead of deleting it, so you keep its settings.

Next steps

With a server saved, set up how you sign in over at Authentication and SSH keys, or learn how your saved servers travel between devices in iCloud sync and Keychain.

docs/authentication-and-keys.heading: Authentication and SSH keys
docs/authentication-and-keys.intro: VVTerm signs in with a password, an SSH key, or an SSH key protected by a passphrase. Here is how each method works and where your credentials are stored.
docs/authentication-and-keys.title: Authentication and SSH keys — VVTerm
docs/authentication-and-keys.description: Password, SSH key, and SSH key with passphrase authentication in VVTerm, and how credentials are kept in the Apple Keychain rather than synced metadata.
docs/authentication-and-keys.schemaDescription: VVTerm authentication methods explained: password, SSH key, and SSH key with passphrase, plus how credentials are stored in the Apple Keychain.
docs/authentication-and-keys.bodyHtml:
Authentication is set per server, so different machines can use different methods. VVTerm supports three options, and whichever you choose, the secret itself is stored in the Apple Keychain rather than in the server definition that syncs through iCloud.

Authentication methods

  • Password — you enter the account password for the server. It is the quickest way to confirm that a host, port, and username are correct, and a fine choice for machines you control. The password is saved to the Keychain so you do not retype it each time.
  • SSH key — you authenticate with a private key instead of a password. The matching public key must be present in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file. Key-based login is more secure than a password and supports passwordless sign-in.
  • SSH key + passphrase — the same as an SSH key, but the private key is itself encrypted with a passphrase. Even if the key is exposed, it cannot be used without the passphrase, which adds a layer of protection for sensitive hosts.

Where credentials live

Passwords, private keys, and passphrases are stored in the Apple Keychain. They are not included in the server metadata that VVTerm syncs through iCloud (CloudKit). That means your server list can travel between devices while the secrets stay in the secure, system-managed store.

Credentials sync between your devices only when iCloud Keychain is enabled in iOS or macOS settings. With it on, a key or password saved on one device becomes available on the others. With it off, credentials stay local to the device they were entered on, and you add them again where needed. For the full picture of what syncs and what does not, see iCloud sync and Keychain.

Generating and importing keys

If you do not already have an SSH key, VVTerm can generate one for you. After generating, copy the public key and add it to the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file, then select that key as the server's authentication method. If you have an existing private key, import it into VVTerm and assign it to the server the same way.

A public key on the server is what authorizes a private key on your device. You can reuse one key pair across many servers by placing the same public key in each server's authorized_keys, or keep separate keys per host for tighter control.

Verifying the host

The first time you connect to a server, VVTerm shows the host's key fingerprint. Confirm it matches what you expect before accepting, so you can be sure you are connecting to the right machine and not an impostor. After you trust a host, later connections proceed without prompting unless its key changes.

Next steps

With authentication set up, move on to the SFTP file browser to manage remote files, or revisit Adding a server to tune the connection details.

docs/getting-started.bodyHtml:
VVTerm is a native SSH terminal and SFTP file client for iPhone, iPad, and Mac. It renders the terminal on the GPU with libghostty and connects over SSH with libssh2, so sessions are fast and accurate. Beyond standard SSH, it can reach machines over Mosh, Tailscale SSH, and Cloudflare Tunnel SSH. This page gets you from install to your first prompt.

System requirements

  • iPhone and iPad — iOS or iPadOS 16 or later.
  • Mac — macOS 13 Ventura or later on an Apple Silicon Mac. Intel Macs are not supported.

VVTerm is one app across all three platforms, and your server list follows you between them through iCloud.

Install VVTerm

  1. Open the App Store on your device and install VVTerm.
  2. Launch the app and finish the short welcome flow.
  3. VVTerm opens to an empty server list, ready for your first connection.

Add your first server

You need three details from the server you want to reach: its host, your username, and how you authenticate.

  1. Start a new server and give it a recognizable name.
  2. Enter the host — a hostname like example.com or an IP like 192.168.1.20.
  3. Set the port. SSH uses 22 by default; change it only if your server listens elsewhere.
  4. Enter the username you log in with, such as root or ubuntu.
  5. Choose an authentication method — password, an SSH key, or an SSH key with a passphrase.

For a full walkthrough of every field and how servers fit into workspaces, see Adding a server.

Connect

  1. Save the server and select it from your list.
  2. The first time you connect to a host, VVTerm shows its key fingerprint so you can verify the host before trusting it.
  3. Once accepted, the terminal opens at the shell prompt and you can start working.

On iPhone and iPad, a keyboard toolbar above the software keyboard adds Esc, Tab, Ctrl, arrow keys, and function keys that terminals depend on. On Mac, full keyboard handling works as you would expect from a native app.

Free vs Pro

VVTerm is free to use, with limits that suit a single machine:

  • Free — one workspace, one server, and one connection tab.
  • Pro — unlimited workspaces, servers, and connection tabs.

Pro is $6.49 per month or $24.99 per year, with a one-time lifetime purchase at $49.99. Purchases, billing, and refunds are handled by Apple through your App Store account. When you are ready to organize more machines, see Workspaces, environments, and tabs.

docs/icloud-sync.heading: iCloud sync and Keychain
docs/icloud-sync.intro: Your server list follows you between iPhone, iPad, and Mac through iCloud, while passwords and SSH keys stay in the Apple Keychain. Here is exactly what syncs and what does not.
docs/icloud-sync.title: iCloud sync and Keychain — VVTerm
docs/icloud-sync.description: VVTerm syncs server metadata through iCloud while passwords and SSH keys stay in the Apple Keychain, syncing only through iCloud Keychain when you enable it.
docs/icloud-sync.schemaDescription: How VVTerm syncs server metadata through iCloud while keeping passwords and SSH keys in the Apple Keychain, how deduplication works, and what does not sync.
docs/icloud-sync.bodyHtml:
VVTerm keeps your setup consistent across devices by splitting your data into two parts: the server definitions that describe how to connect, and the secrets used to sign in. They are handled differently on purpose, so your list can travel freely while your credentials stay protected.

What syncs through iCloud

Server metadata syncs through iCloud using CloudKit. That includes the details you enter when adding a server — its name, host, port, username, and environment — along with your workspaces and how everything is organized. Add a server on your Mac and it appears on your iPhone and iPad; rename a workspace on one device and the change follows to the others.

What stays in the Keychain

Your secrets — passwords, private SSH keys, and passphrases — are stored in the Apple Keychain, not in the synced metadata. They are deliberately kept out of CloudKit, so the part of your data that moves through iCloud never contains a credential.

Credentials move between your devices only when iCloud Keychain is enabled in your iOS or macOS settings. With it on, a saved password or key becomes available on your other devices through Apple's secure Keychain sync. With it off, credentials stay on the device where you entered them, and you add them again on each device you use.

What does not sync

  • Credentials are never carried by CloudKit. Passwords and SSH keys are excluded from the synced server metadata entirely.
  • If iCloud Keychain is off, your secrets do not leave the device, even though the server list still syncs.
  • Active terminal sessions and connection tabs are local to a device and are not synced.

Deduplication

Each server and workspace carries a stable identifier. When VVTerm merges changes coming from iCloud, it matches records by ID, so the same server that exists on two devices is reconciled into a single entry rather than duplicated. This keeps your list clean even when you make edits on more than one device.

Working without iCloud

If iCloud is unavailable or turned off, VVTerm falls back to local storage so the app keeps working on that device. Your servers are saved locally and remain usable; they simply will not propagate to your other devices until iCloud sync is available again.

Next steps

To control how secrets are stored per server, see Authentication and SSH keys. To organize the servers that sync, see Workspaces, environments, and tabs.

docs/sftp-file-browser.heading: Using the SFTP file browser
docs/sftp-file-browser.intro: VVTerm includes a built-in SFTP browser so you can move, preview, and edit remote files without a separate app. Here is how to use it.
docs/sftp-file-browser.title: Using the SFTP file browser — VVTerm

docs/sftp-file-browser.schemaDescription: Use the VVTerm SFTP file browser to browse remote folders, upload and download, create directories, rename, move, delete, preview, and edit files and permissions.
docs/sftp-file-browser.bodyHtml:
Every server you connect to over SSH can also be browsed over SFTP in the same app. The file browser runs on top of your existing connection, so there is nothing extra to configure on the server — if you can SSH in, you can manage files.

Opening the file browser

From a connected server, open the Files view to start browsing. VVTerm lists the remote directory contents, showing names, sizes, and types. On Mac the browser sits beside your terminal in the same window; on iPhone and iPad it opens as its own view so you can switch between the shell and your files.

Browsing folders

  • Tap or click a folder to open it, and use the path or back navigation to move up.
  • Start from your home directory and walk into any path your account can read.
  • Items you do not have permission to enter are limited by the server, just as they would be in a shell.

Uploading and downloading

Move files in both directions directly from the browser:

  • Download a remote file to your device to keep a local copy.
  • Upload a file from your device to the current remote folder.

This is the quickest way to pull down a log, push up a config, or move assets between machines without dropping to a command line.

Managing files and folders

  • Create folders to organize remote directories.
  • Rename files and folders in place.
  • Move items to a different path.
  • Delete files and folders you no longer need.

These actions run over SFTP against the live server, so changes take effect immediately.

Previewing files

You can preview common file types without downloading them first. VVTerm renders text, images, and video inline, which makes it easy to check a file's contents — confirm a config, glance at a screenshot, or scrub a recording — before deciding what to do with it.

Editing text files

For text files, the browser includes an editor so you can make a quick change to a config or script and save it straight back to the server. There is no need to copy a file down, edit it locally, and upload it again for small edits.

Editing permissions

On servers that support it, you can view and change a file's POSIX permissions — the read, write, and execute bits for owner, group, and others. This is handy for making a script executable or tightening access on a sensitive file without typing chmod by hand.

Next steps

File access depends on the account you log in as, set in Adding a server and Authentication and SSH keys. To keep your servers consistent across devices, see iCloud sync and Keychain.

docs/workspaces-and-tabs.intro: Workspaces and environments keep your servers organized, while connection tabs let you run more than one session at once. Here is how the pieces fit together.

docs/workspaces-and-tabs.bodyHtml:
As you add more machines, VVTerm gives you two ways to keep them organized — workspaces and environments — and connection tabs so you can work in several sessions at once. They sync across your devices through iCloud, so your organization is the same everywhere.

Workspaces

A workspace is the top-level group your servers belong to. Use one per client, per project, or per team to keep unrelated machines apart. Every server lives inside exactly one workspace, and switching workspaces changes which servers you see. Workspaces sync through iCloud along with the servers they contain.

Environments

Within a workspace, an environment sorts servers further — for example Production, Staging, or Development. Environments let you filter a busy list down to the machines you care about right now, and they keep production hosts visually distinct from the ones you can experiment on. You set a server's environment when adding or editing it.

Connection tabs

A connection tab is a single live session with a server. Opening a server starts a tab; opening another server, or the same server again, starts a second tab. Each tab is independent, so you can run a long task in one while you work in another.

Switch between tabs to move from one session to the next without disconnecting. On Mac, tabs live in the unified toolbar; on iPhone and iPad you move between your open connections from the session view.

Free and Pro limits

VVTerm's tiers control how much you can organize and how many sessions you can run at once:

  • Free — one workspace, one server, and one connection tab.
  • Pro — unlimited workspaces, servers, and connection tabs.

With Pro you can keep several connections open at the same time — for example a production shell, a staging shell, and an SFTP session — and group them across as many workspaces and environments as you need. faqItems.question: How does VVTerm keep my session alive?
faqItems.answer: On connect, VVTerm creates or attaches a managed tmux session on the server. Because the session lives on the remote host, your work keeps running even after the connection drops — VVTerm reattaches to it the next time you connect.

faqItems.question: Do I have to install or configure tmux myself?
faqItems.answer: No. If tmux isn't installed, VVTerm installs it with the host's package manager. It also writes a tuned config to ~/.vvterm/tmux.conf — true color, mouse support, a large scrollback buffer, and smart scroll that uses copy mode at the shell but passes through inside full-screen apps.

faqItems.question: Can I reconnect to a session I started earlier?
faqItems.answer: Yes. VVTerm lists existing sessions with their window counts and attached clients, so you can reattach to the one you want or clean up old detached sessions.

faqItems.question: What if I prefer a plain shell?
faqItems.answer: Set tmux startup to Skip globally, or override it on a single server. You can also choose Ask every time so VVTerm prompts when you open a new tab or split.

faqItems.question: Is this the same as tmux control mode?
faqItems.answer: No. VVTerm orchestrates a real tmux session over a normal shell for persistence and reconnects — it does not run tmux control mode (-CC).

faqItems.question: Does it work on Windows servers?
faqItems.answer: Yes. On Windows and PowerShell hosts VVTerm uses psmux for the same persistence, and can install it with winget, scoop, choco, or cargo.

guides/cloudflare-tunnel-ssh-setup.heading: Connect over Cloudflare Tunnel SSH
guides/cloudflare-tunnel-ssh-setup.intro: SSH to a server behind Cloudflare Tunnel from VVTerm by its public hostname — with no inbound ports open on the host.
guides/cloudflare-tunnel-ssh-setup.title: Connect over Cloudflare Tunnel SSH — VVTerm
guides/cloudflare-tunnel-ssh-setup.description: Configure cloudflared for SSH, publish a public hostname, and connect from VVTerm to a server behind Cloudflare Tunnel with no inbound ports open.
guides/cloudflare-tunnel-ssh-setup.schemaDescription: Step-by-step guide to SSH over Cloudflare Tunnel with VVTerm: configure cloudflared for SSH, publish a public hostname, and connect to it with no inbound ports open.
guides/cloudflare-tunnel-ssh-setup.bodyHtml:
Cloudflare Tunnel lets a server expose a service through Cloudflare's network without opening any inbound ports. VVTerm can connect to an SSH service published this way using its public hostname, so a host behind NAT or a strict firewall stays reachable.

How it works

A lightweight cloudflared daemon on the server makes an outbound connection to Cloudflare and registers a route. Cloudflare then maps a public hostname to your local SSH service. Because the tunnel is established from the inside out, the host never needs an open inbound port — there is nothing to expose or forward.

Prerequisites

  1. A Cloudflare account with a domain managed in Cloudflare.
  2. cloudflared installed on the server, and a named tunnel created and authenticated.
  3. The tunnel configured for SSH, routing a public hostname to the local SSH service at localhost:22.

In a typical cloudflared config, an ingress rule maps the hostname to SSH, for example: 

ingress:
  - hostname: ssh.example.com
    service: ssh://localhost:22
  - service: http_status:404

Add the public hostname as a DNS route for the tunnel, then run the tunnel so the route goes live. If you use Cloudflare Access in front of the hostname, make sure your policy permits the user that will be connecting.

Connect from VVTerm

  1. In VVTerm, tap Add Server (or edit an existing server).
  2. Set the host to your tunnel's public hostname, for example ssh.example.com.
  3. Enter the username you log in with on the server, and keep your usual SSH authentication — password or key.
  4. Choose Cloudflare Tunnel SSH as the connection method.
  5. Save and tap the server to connect.

VVTerm reaches the hostname through Cloudflare and lands you at the server's shell, just like a direct SSH session.

No inbound ports open

The advantage of this setup is what you don't have to do: no port 22 exposed to the internet, no firewall rule for inbound SSH, and no router configuration. The only network connection the host initiates is outbound to Cloudflare, which keeps the attack surface small.

Troubleshooting

  • If the hostname won't connect, confirm the tunnel is running and that its ingress rule points at ssh://localhost:22.
  • Check that the public hostname has a DNS route attached to the tunnel in the Cloudflare dashboard.
  • If access is blocked, review any Cloudflare Access policy covering the hostname.

guides/how-to-ssh-from-iphone.heading: How to SSH into a server from your iPhone
guides/how-to-ssh-from-iphone.intro: Add a server, pick an authentication method, and open your first secure shell session on iOS — then drive it with the on-screen keyboard toolbar.
guides/how-to-ssh-from-iphone.title: How to SSH from iPhone — VVTerm
guides/how-to-ssh-from-iphone.description: Install VVTerm, add a server, choose password or SSH key auth, connect, and use the keyboard toolbar to SSH into any server from your iPhone.

guides/how-to-ssh-from-iphone.bodyHtml:
VVTerm turns your iPhone into a full SSH client. You can reach any server that accepts SSH — a Linux box, a Mac, a Raspberry Pi, a cloud VM — and work in a real GPU-rendered terminal. This guide walks through the first connection end to end.

Before you start

You need an iPhone running iOS 16 or later and a server you can reach over the network. Have three things ready: the server's hostname or IP address, the port (SSH uses 22 by default), and your username. If you authenticate with a key instead of a password, have the private key available too.

Install VVTerm

  1. Open the App Store on your iPhone and install VVTerm.
  2. Launch the app and finish the short welcome flow.

The free tier includes one server, which is all you need to follow this guide. Pro removes the limits when you want more servers, workspaces, and connection tabs.

Add your server

  1. Tap Add Server to open the new-server form.
  2. Give the server a name so it's easy to recognize later.
  3. Enter the host — a hostname like example.com or an IP like 192.168.1.20.
  4. Set the port. Leave it at 22 unless your server listens elsewhere.
  5. Enter the username you log in with, for example root or ubuntu.

Choose an authentication method

VVTerm supports three ways to authenticate, and your credentials are stored in the Apple Keychain — never in synced metadata.

  • Password — enter the account password. Simple, and a good way to test that the host and username are correct.
  • SSH key — use a private key for passwordless, more secure login. Paste or import the key, and make sure the matching public key is in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
  • SSH key + passphrase — the same as above, but the private key is itself encrypted with a passphrase for an extra layer of protection.

If you don't have a key yet, VVTerm can generate one for you. Add the generated public key to the server's authorized_keys file, then select that key as the server's auth method.

Connect

  1. Save the server. It appears in your server list.
  2. Tap the server to open a connection.
  3. The first time you connect, VVTerm shows the host's key fingerprint so you can verify it before trusting the host.
  4. Once accepted, the terminal opens and you land at the shell prompt.

Use the keyboard toolbar

The iOS software keyboard is missing keys that terminals rely on, so VVTerm adds an accessory toolbar directly above it. From there you get:

  • Esc — essential for vim, less, and most TUI apps.
  • Tab — shell and path completion.
  • Ctrl — tap it, then a letter, to send control sequences like Ctrl-C or Ctrl-Z.
  • Arrow keys — move the cursor and walk through command history.
  • Function keys — F1 through F12 for apps that map them.

You can customize the toolbar with your own command snippets, so frequently used commands are one tap away.

Next steps

Your session can survive network drops if you keep it alive with tmux, and you can reach servers that aren't directly exposed using Mosh, Tailscale SSH, or Cloudflare Tunnel SSH. When you need to move files, see SFTP file transfer on iOS.

guides/set-up-mosh-on-ios.heading: Set up Mosh on iPhone and iPad
guides/set-up-mosh-on-ios.intro: Mosh keeps SSH sessions alive across network drops, sleep, and IP changes. Here's how to prepare your server and enable Mosh in VVTerm.
guides/set-up-mosh-on-ios.title: Set up Mosh on iPhone and iPad — VVTerm
guides/set-up-mosh-on-ios.description: Install mosh-server, open the UDP ports, and enable Mosh for a server in VVTerm to keep SSH sessions alive across network drops, sleep, and IP changes on iOS.
guides/set-up-mosh-on-ios.schemaDescription: Step-by-step guide to using Mosh with VVTerm on iOS and iPadOS: install mosh-server, open UDP ports, enable Mosh for a server, and connect with roaming sessions.
guides/set-up-mosh-on-ios.bodyHtml:
On a phone or tablet your network changes constantly — Wi-Fi to cellular, a tunnel into the subway, the screen locking. A plain SSH session dies on each of those. Mosh solves it, and VVTerm has it built in.

What Mosh is

Mosh (mobile shell) is a remote terminal protocol designed for unreliable, mobile connections. Compared with plain SSH it adds:

  • Roaming — the session follows you as your IP address changes, so switching from Wi-Fi to cellular doesn't drop it.
  • Survives drops and sleep — close the lid or lose signal, and the session reconnects when you're back instead of hanging dead.
  • Local echo — your keystrokes appear instantly even on a high-latency link, with corrections applied as the server replies.
  • SSH fallback — Mosh uses SSH to authenticate and start the session, then hands off to its own UDP transport.

Prepare the server

Mosh runs a small helper on the host, so it has to be installed there first.

  1. SSH into the server and install the Mosh package. On Debian or Ubuntu: 
    sudo apt install mosh
    On RHEL, Fedora, or CentOS use sudo dnf install mosh, and on macOS use brew install mosh.
  2. This provides mosh-server, which VVTerm launches over SSH each time you connect.

Open the UDP ports

Mosh does not use TCP port 22 for its data — it uses UDP, by default in the range 60000–61000. If a firewall sits in front of the server, allow inbound UDP on that range.

  1. With UFW on Ubuntu: 
    sudo ufw allow 60000:61000/udp
  2. On a cloud provider, add the same UDP range to the instance's security group or firewall rules.

SSH on its usual TCP port must stay reachable too, because Mosh authenticates over SSH before starting its UDP session.

Enable Mosh in VVTerm

  1. Open the server's settings in VVTerm — either when adding it or by editing an existing server.
  2. Switch the connection method to Mosh.
  3. Keep your existing SSH authentication; Mosh reuses it to start the session.
  4. Save, then tap the server to connect.

VVTerm opens an SSH connection, starts mosh-server on the host, and then carries your session over Mosh's UDP transport.

What you'll notice on a network change

With Mosh active, the experience changes in a few visible ways. Typing feels instant thanks to local echo, even on a slow link. When you switch networks or wake the device, the session reconnects on its own — no re-login, no lost shell. If the connection is briefly unreachable, VVTerm shows the session as waiting and resumes it once the network returns.

Tips

  • Pair Mosh with tmux for the strongest setup: Mosh survives the trip to the server, and tmux preserves your work even if the server itself restarts the session.
  • If a connection won't start, confirm mosh-server is installed and the UDP range is open — those are the two most common causes.

guides/sftp-file-transfer-on-ios.bodyHtml:
Every server you connect to in VVTerm also has a built-in SFTP file browser, so you can manage remote files without leaving the app or installing a separate client. It works over the same SSH connection you already use.

Open the file browser

  1. Connect to a server as usual.
  2. Open the Files view for that connection to switch from the terminal to the SFTP browser.
  3. VVTerm lists the contents of a starting directory — typically your home folder — over SFTP.

Browse remote folders

Tap a folder to open it and use the path or back control to move up the tree. Files show their names and details so you can find what you need. Browsing is read-only until you choose to transfer or change something, so there's no risk in simply looking around.

Upload and download

  • Download a remote file to your device when you want a local copy, for example to save it into the Files app or share it elsewhere.
  • Upload a file from your iPhone or iPad into the current remote folder to push it to the server.

Transfers run over the encrypted SSH connection, so files never leave a secured channel.

Manage files and folders

The browser handles the everyday file operations you'd expect on the server:

  • Create folders to organize remote directories.
  • Rename files and folders in place.
  • Move items to a different directory.
  • Delete files and folders you no longer need.

Preview without downloading

You can preview many files directly in VVTerm before deciding what to do with them — text files, images, and video — so you can check a config file or a screenshot without first pulling it onto your device.

Edit text and permissions

  1. Open a supported text file to edit it in place, then save the changes straight back to the server over SFTP.
  2. Adjust a file or folder's POSIX permissions — the read, write, and execute bits for owner, group, and others — when you need to fix access without dropping into the shell.

Tips

  • For quick config tweaks, editing a file in the SFTP browser is often faster than opening an editor in the terminal.
  • Use preview to confirm you have the right file before downloading or deleting it.
  • The same SFTP browser is available on iPhone, iPad, and Mac, so the workflow carries across all your devices.

VVTerm for Mac is a native SSH terminal built like the rest of macOS — a split-view sidebar of your servers next to a GPU-rendered terminal, with a unified toolbar for tabs. This guide covers your first connection on the Mac.

Before you start

You need a Mac with Apple Silicon running macOS 13 Ventura or later. Have your server's host, port (22 by default), and username ready, plus a password or SSH key for authentication.

Install VVTerm

  1. Install VVTerm from the App Store on your Mac.
  2. Open the app. The window shows a sidebar for your servers and a detail area for the terminal.

Add a server in the sidebar

  1. Tap Add Server to open the new-server form.
  2. Enter a name, the host, the port, and your username.
  3. Optionally organize servers into workspaces and environments so larger fleets stay tidy in the sidebar.
  4. Save. The server appears in the sidebar list.

Choose an authentication method

Pick how you want to log in. Whatever you choose, the secret itself is stored in the macOS Keychain, not in synced server metadata.

  • Password — enter the account password directly.
  • SSH key — import or generate a private key and add the matching public key to the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
  • SSH key + passphrase — use an encrypted private key protected by a passphrase.

Connect in a tab

  1. Select the server in the sidebar to open a connection.
  2. Confirm the host key fingerprint the first time you connect.
  3. The terminal opens in the detail area, drawn on Metal by libghostty for true color and accurate output.

Open multiple tabs and panes

Each connection lives in a tab in the unified toolbar, so you can keep several servers open at once and switch between them. You can also split a tab into panes for side-by-side shells on the same screen.

The free tier includes one connection tab. Pro unlocks unlimited tabs and split panes — $6.49/month, $24.99/year, or a $49.99 lifetime purchase, handled through Apple.

Your servers sync over iCloud

Server metadata — names, hosts, ports, usernames, and workspaces — syncs through iCloud, so a server you add on your Mac shows up on your iPhone and iPad automatically. Passwords and SSH keys are not part of that metadata; they stay in the Apple Keychain and only travel between devices through iCloud Keychain when you enable it.

Next steps

guides/tailscale-ssh-setup.heading: Connect with Tailscale SSH
guides/tailscale-ssh-setup.intro: Reach machines on your tailnet by their MagicDNS name from VVTerm — no port forwarding, no exposed ports, and no extra SSH keys to manage.
guides/tailscale-ssh-setup.title: Connect with Tailscale SSH — VVTerm
guides/tailscale-ssh-setup.description: Enable Tailscale SSH on your host with tailscale up --ssh, set ACLs, and connect to the MagicDNS name from VVTerm — no port forwarding or exposed ports.

guides/tailscale-ssh-setup.bodyHtml:
Tailscale puts your devices on a private mesh network and can handle SSH authentication for you with Tailscale SSH. With it, you reach a server by its tailnet name from VVTerm — no public ports, no port forwarding, and no separate SSH keys to distribute.

How it works

Every machine you join to your tailnet gets a stable private address and a MagicDNS name like myserver.tailnet-name.ts.net. When Tailscale SSH is enabled, Tailscale itself authenticates connections between devices in your tailnet based on your access policy, so the server never needs an inbound port open to the public internet.

Prerequisites

  1. A Tailscale account with the host and your iPhone, iPad, or Mac both joined to the same tailnet.
  2. Tailscale installed on the host you want to reach.
  3. Tailscale running on the device you're connecting from, signed into the same account.

Enable Tailscale SSH on the host

  1. On the server, bring Tailscale up with the SSH flag: 
    sudo tailscale up --ssh
  2. This advertises the host as accepting Tailscale SSH connections. Authentication is handled by Tailscale rather than by traditional SSH keys.
  3. Confirm the host's tailnet name and status: 
    tailscale status

Allow SSH in your ACLs

Tailscale SSH access is governed by the SSH rules in your tailnet's access control policy. In the Tailscale admin console, make sure your policy includes an ssh section that permits your user to reach the host as the desired login user. Without a matching rule, the connection is refused even though the host is online. Save the policy before you connect.

Connect from VVTerm

  1. In VVTerm, tap Add Server (or edit an existing server).
  2. Set the host to the machine's MagicDNS name, for example myserver.tailnet-name.ts.net. You can also use its tailnet IP address.
  3. Keep the port at 22 and enter the username you want to log in as on the host.
  4. Choose Tailscale SSH as the connection method so authentication is handled through your tailnet.
  5. Save and tap the server to connect.

No port forwarding required

Because traffic rides the encrypted tailnet, you do not open port 22 to the internet, configure a router, or punch holes in a firewall. The host can sit behind NAT or a strict firewall and still be reachable from your devices, anywhere they have a connection.

Troubleshooting

  • If the name doesn't resolve, confirm MagicDNS is enabled for your tailnet and that the host shows as connected in tailscale status.
  • If you connect but get permission denied, revisit your ACL ssh rules and the login user you requested.
  • If the device can't see the host at all, make sure both are signed into the same Tailscale account and online.

faqItems.question: What does VVTerm for iPad need to run?
faqItems.answer: iPadOS 16 or later. The terminal renders on Metal, so a modern iPad gives the smoothest results.

faqItems.answer: No. VVTerm is built around the keyboard and touch. A hardware keyboard such as the Magic Keyboard makes shell work fastest, and the on-screen terminal toolbar covers the keys iPadOS would otherwise hide.

faqItems.answer: The terminal keyboard toolbar sits above the on-screen keyboard with Esc, Tab, Ctrl, arrow keys, and function keys. With a hardware keyboard the physical keys map straight through.

faqItems.answer: Yes. Run VVTerm in Stage Manager beside other apps, and connect an external display for a larger workspace. Mosh keeps the session alive as you move around.

faqItems.question: Will my session survive switching from Wi-Fi to cellular?
faqItems.answer: With Mosh, yes. Mosh roams across network changes and sleep and reconnects on its own, falling back to standard SSH when you prefer it.

faqItems.answer: VVTerm manages a tmux session on the server, so a running command keeps going even after the connection drops, and reattaches the next time you connect — it installs tmux for you if it's missing.

faqItems.question: Can I customize the keyboard toolbar?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Choose which keys appear and add your own command snippets (insert text, optionally with Enter) and shortcuts (a key with Ctrl, Alt, Cmd, or Shift). Your layout syncs across devices through iCloud.

faqItems.question: Can I monitor server load on iPad?
faqItems.answer: Yes. Live monitoring shows CPU, memory, network, disk, load average, and top processes in real time over your existing SSH session.

faqItems.question: How much does VVTerm cost?
